item.title: The story we need
item.description:
-

Times like this, we need stories. Personally, I like a nice heartwarming story about a kid and a horse. Or when kids get in over their heads and take on a little more than we think they’re capable of. Those are nice stories. They make me feel good. But feeling good doesn’t get you out of trouble. More often than not, it let’s you ignore the trouble until it’s knocking on your door. Even then, it can be tempting to hold your breath and mute the tv and duck under the covers - crouch and watch for shadows to stop moving under the door. Times like this we need a story about a person that’s just trying to keep his head down and be a worker among workers. You see this guy and he seems a little meek, but you’ve seen stories like this and your gut tells you that he’s just trying not to do something that’ll have consequences beyond his control. This guy has a past he isn’t all that comfortable with but, more than likely, afforded him a certain set of charater traits and skills that have a certain value in difficult circumstances. Liam Neeson’s warning to his daughter’s kidnapper i Taken captures this well - “a very particular set of skills. Skills I have acquired over a very long career. Skills that make me a nightmare for people like you. . .” But these anti-heroes are always former elite-something-or-others: a gunfighter, a space coyboy, a Navy SEAL, some kind of hacker that was at MIT when he was 8. Such a resume gives the writer some freedom to get the character out of seemingly-impossible situations - situations that are impossible for the layperson. But most of us are laypeople, or, more accurately, I am but I am also not totally helpless. That said, we are all helpless in many matters. item.title: Guilty Pleasures
item.description: The blanket acceptance of using the term ‘guilty pleasure’ to excuse our indulgence of things that aren’t collectively considered cool, classy, or otherwise justifiable is an efficient indicator of how necessary these transgressions of taste are. The longer you’re alive, or, rather, the more experiences you cobble together, the less control you have over the things that hold meaning for you and, thus, become indulgences. Only from the safe, sterile perch of the critic’s desk can one maintain a proper set of standards for art and food and music or anything else. As I get older, though, I am beginning to wonder if these guilty ones have the most meat. They end up being the little splashes of color that decorate your brutalist, non-descript cubicle that your life can become when you’re not paying attention. IF you’re thoughtful, you start to find that your tastes are arguably more defined than the so-called critic’s - that lived experience trumps the academic every time.

item.title: Nobody Move, Nobody Gets Hurt
item.description: This is everyone’s favorite part of the bank job. Our guys - we’re usually rooting for the robbers - are letting everyone know that they have no intention of committing wanton violence; they’re here for the bank’s money, not your money. You have no reason to be a hero, it will gain you nothing and we’ll be forced to maintain control whatever means necessary. If you do not cooperate, people will get hurt, it will be your fault, and we’ll all be back where we started but with more bumps, bruises, or holes in us. The likelihood of experiencing this particular situation is low. I would love to watch a gang of tactically competent, smooth-ass criminals walk out of a bank with bags of money. What is much more likely is that it a the tacit warning from an adversary, an abuser, or an oppressor. “Behave.” “Don’t make me hurt you.” “Don’t force me to respond.” “Do not make waves.” “Do what you’re told or there will be consequences.” More palatably, “everything is fine, just sit still. We’ve got this covered.” There a video of Sinead doing “The Emporer’s New Clothes” from 1990 you can find on YouTube. It is a stellar performance of a supreme talent and ferocious character owning a stage. She rattles off the words “nobody move, nobody gets hurt” three times at the song’s conclusion. I think it is a fair critique to comment that the likely sentiment is “if nobody moves, nobody gets hurt.” But I will stick be her version since I had it tattooed on my shoulders.

I miss my brother. He died suddenly a year ago today. It probably didn’t feel sudden to him, and it wasn’t much of a surprise to anyone else who had witnessed his struggles over what feels like the entirety of his adult life. I sought counseling to help with the loss but it was more to determine if I was, in fact, coping with it. We determined that I had and was but I’m not so sure anymore. My memories of him are mostly stale. I saw him about a month before he died and we had a nice time. He seemed like he was getting to a good place. But as a person who has long-term sobriety and who struggled greatly with addiction, I was, of course skeptical nad measured in my enthusiasm about his recovery.
